entries.narration: Sun is a pay television and broadband company. It's made up for this course, but built the way such companies really work. On Saturday the thirty first of October, its biggest live event of the month is on: the Northbridge versus Eastfield derby. This picture follows one night of viewing from left to right. On the left is a household, one of five thousand. It watches on a set top box in the living room, and on the app, on a phone, a tablet or a browser. In the middle is what those devices send. A message when the picture starts, called play. A heartbeat every minute it keeps playing. Buffer, when the picture stalls. And stop, when it ends. Across every device, that one Saturday adds up to just over four hundred thousand events. On the right is Sun, with the two things it needs to know. While the match is on, how many households are watching each channel, minute by minute. And next morning, how each title really performed, correctly, per region and per exchange. Along the bottom is the part viewers never see. Every household's line runs to one of twelve broadband exchanges, and each exchange reports on itself every minute. When one exchange struggles, the picture stalls in every home it serves. That's why viewing and network data have to be read together. Next, the two answers themselves, and why they need two different clocks.

Here are both answers this whole course builds towards, computed the simplest possible way, so we know exactly what the platform has to reproduce. The file is derby dot p y. It reads every viewing event of the night. For each minute, it collects the households seen watching the derby. For each broadband exchange, it adds up the seconds watched and the milliseconds spent buffering. The terminal shows the results. The first answer is live: the derby peaked at two thousand one hundred and forty households, at eighteen forty one, U T C. The second is for next morning: buffering divided by watching time, per exchange. One exchange, L D N zero four, buffered four point one percent of the time. Every other exchange was at zero point six. The side pane plots the first answer as a curve. It climbs from kick off, dips at half time, peaks in the second half, and falls away after the final whistle. Below it, the table of ratios, with L D N zero four marked. The card at the bottom says why this script isn't the platform. It ran on one laptop, over every event at once, after the match was over. The live answer has to arrive while the match is still being played, from events that come in late and out of order. The next morning answer has to be correct and reconciled, every night, without anyone running a script. Next, the platform that does both, on Google Cloud.

This is the whole platform, called viewing pulse, as it will look at the end of the course. Every part of it is created by Terraform, inside one Google Cloud project in London. On the left are Sun's own systems: the C R M, billing, the vendors' catalogue and programme guide, and the households' devices. The project has two lanes, one for each clock. The top lane is the nightly batch, built for correctness. Each night's extracts land in a raw zone in Cloud Storage. BigQuery loads them into Bronze, exactly as received. Silver holds the cleaned, deduplicated data, and Gold holds the marts the business reads. Dataproc runs the heavy join between viewing and network quality. Gates sit on the arrows, G one to G four, and a night that fails one goes no further. The bottom lane is live, built for speed. Every device's events arrive on Pub Sub. Dataflow counts viewers per channel per minute, in event time, and writes the live table in BigQuery. Both lanes end at Looker, where the business reads the live curve during the match and the reconciled numbers next morning. Along the bottom are the services the whole platform depends on: I A M and its service accounts, Secret Manager, Cloud K M S, Composer to run the nightly schedule, Dataplex, Sensitive Data Protection, Logging, Monitoring, Cloud Build and a budget. Each service is introduced only when the platform first needs it. Next, how Google Cloud itself is built.

Before anything is built, it helps to know where it will physically live. Google Cloud is divided into regions, and each region into zones, and the platform's every regional resource will sit in one place: europe west two, London. This is a read only lab, recorded once on the project, and it creates nothing. In the terminal, the first command counts Google's regions: forty three. The second asks about London's, and its status is up. The third lists the zones inside it: europe west two a, b and c. The side pane draws what those answers mean. Around the outside is Google's network, with all forty three regions joined by its own private network. Inside, the London region, and inside that, three zones. A zone is a separate part of the region, with its own power, cooling and networking, so trouble in one shouldn't take down the others. The table below shows what that means for the resources in this course. A zonal resource, like a single Dataproc worker, lives in one zone and doesn't survive that zone failing. A regional one, like a bucket, a BigQuery dataset or a K M S key, is spread across the region's zones and survives a zone failing. Global resources, like I A M and the project itself, don't belong to any one region. Next, what owns all of these resources: the project, and whatever sits above it.

Every Google Cloud resource belongs to exactly one project, and projects can sit inside folders, which sit inside an organization. That hierarchy decides where billing goes, which A P Is are on, and how permissions flow down. This lab reads it. The first command describes the project. Its i d is sun media dev, the name people use. Its number is a long numeral that Google uses internally, and it will turn up in service account names and error messages. The parent field is missing, and the second command shows why. Asking for the project's ancestors returns one line: the project itself. There is no folder and no organization above it. The side pane draws the full hierarchy anyway, with the two missing levels greyed out. In a company, the organization at the top would usually be the company's domain, folders would group teams or environments, and policies set up there would flow down into every project beneath. Here there is just the project, and below it the resources the course will create: buckets, datasets, topics and keys, each belonging to this project alone. The card at the bottom gives the reason a project matters so much. It's the unit of billing, of A P Is, and of identity and access. A course that builds its whole platform in one project can tear it down cleanly afterwards. Next, the A P Is: every service is switched on, project by project.

Every Google Cloud service is an A P I, and a project can only call the A P Is switched on for it. This lab shows a call refused, then the switch flipped, then the same call working. The first command counts the A P Is already enabled on the project: fifty two. Compute Engine is not one of them. So the second command, a request to list London's zones, is refused. The error is long but precise. The Compute Engine A P I has not been used in this project before, or it's disabled. It gives the reason, service disabled, and a link to enable it. The third command switches it on, and the operation finishes successfully. The fourth repeats the first call, and now it returns London's three zones. The side pane draws that sequence. The project and its enabled A P Is. Compute switched off, and the call refused. The switch flipped, for this project only. Then the same call answered. Switching on an A P I creates nothing and costs nothing by itself. It only allows the project to make the calls. The card at the bottom records a rule this course keeps. This one switch is made with the command line, while the course is still exploring. From the next course on, Terraform switches on whatever A P Is the platform needs, as code, alongside the resources that use them. Next, two different kinds of request to the same service.

Every service has two kinds of request. Some manage the resource itself, and some use what it holds. They're called the control plane and the data plane, and they're often governed by different permissions. This lab uses Google's public sample bucket, which anyone may read, so nothing in the project is touched. The first describe asks for the bucket's settings: it's in the U S, in the multi regional storage class. Then the same describe runs with dash dash log H T T P, which prints every request g cloud sends, filtered to the address. It went to storage slash v one slash b, then the bucket's name: the bucket as a resource. Listing the bucket the same way went somewhere else: the same path, followed by slash o, the bucket's objects. The last command counts forty six entries at the top level. The side pane splits the two planes. On the left, the control plane: the bucket's own address, and the kind of work done there, which is creating, configuring and setting policy. That's what Terraform does. On the right, the data plane: the objects' address, and reading, writing and listing. That's what the pipeline does. The table shows the two addresses g cloud called. This split comes back throughout the course. The extract's service account will be allowed to write objects into the raw zone, but never to change the bucket's settings. Next, three different clients, all calling the same A P I.

The Cloud Console, the g cloud command line and Terraform look like three different tools, but they're three clients of the same R E S T A P Is. This lab reads one thing, the project, three ways, and shows they all arrive at the same place. First g cloud, with logging on. It sent a G E T request to the Cloud Resource Manager A P I: version one, projects, then the project i d. Then the same request with no tool at all. A short lived access token goes into a shell variable, and is never printed. Curl sends it to that address and gets back the project's i d and number. Last, Terraform. A tiny configuration with a single data source reads the same project, creates nothing, and outputs the same i d and number. The side pane draws all of it. On the left are the clients: g cloud, a bare curl with a token, Terraform's Google provider, and the Console, greyed out, because this course never takes screenshots of it. All four arrows land on one service, Cloud Resource Manager, and one request. The table lines up the answers: the same project, and where it was printed, the same number. This is why the course can use g cloud to read and Terraform to build without them ever disagreeing. Underneath, there's only one source of truth, the A P I. Next, the two families of service this platform is built from.

The services this platform uses fall into two families, and knowing which family a service belongs to tells you what you pay for and what you still have to look after. This is a concept frame, drawn from Google Cloud's documentation, and the label at the top cites the pages. On the left is the serverless family. With BigQuery you send a query, and Google finds the machines to run it. With Pub Sub you send a message, and Google stores it and delivers it. With Dataflow you send a pipeline, and Google starts the workers, scales them up and down, and stops them. You pay for what you use: bytes scanned, messages, worker time. On the right are managed clusters. A Dataproc cluster is a set of machines you choose, and it runs, and bills, until you stop it. Composer is the same idea for Airflow: an environment billed by the hour, which is why this course never leaves one running. Between the two sits Dataproc Serverless, a Spark batch with no cluster to keep, and that's the one Course nine uses. The table draws the responsibility line. Google always runs the machines, their patches and the engine. With a cluster, you also decide how many machines there are. And whichever family a service belongs to, the bottom two rows stay yours: your code and its configuration, and your data and who may read it. Next, a month of this platform, measured in the units Google bills by.

Every Google Cloud service bills by some meter, and a platform's cost is mostly a question of which meters it moves, and how far. This frame is a model, and the label says so: one night's real data sizes, multiplied by thirty, plus three assumptions written at the top of the file. It prints quantities, never prices. A price belongs to the pricing page, on the day you read it. The editor shows the assumptions: two hundred dashboard queries a day, a streaming job running six hours a night, and one Dataflow worker with four virtual C P Us. Everything else is measured from the generated data. In the terminal, the month comes out like this. The raw zone stores about forty three megabytes, which is small. Pub Sub carries just over twelve million messages, about three gigabytes. BigQuery scans around six hundred gigabytes, because every dashboard query reads a day of viewing events. And Dataflow runs seven hundred and twenty v C P U hours. The side pane's table repeats those numbers and marks the two that grow fastest. Below it are the three things that move a meter. How much is kept, which is cheap, and cheaper still as data cools. How much is read: BigQuery bills the bytes each query scans, so partitioning, in Course ten, matters more than storage. And how long something runs: workers bill for as long as they exist, so a finished stream job must be drained. With Google Cloud's building blocks in place, the next course meets Sun's sources and makes the first deployment.

Before building anything on Google Cloud, it helps to know exactly what Sun's data looks like and how each piece arrives. The editor holds the project's first file, a readme listing Sun's five sources. The C R M knows the households and their packages. Billing records every charge. The catalogue and the E P G, the programme guide, are files that vendors deliver each day. Viewing events come from every set-top box and every copy of the app: a message when something starts playing, one every minute it plays, and one when it stops. And network telemetry comes from Sun's twelve broadband exchanges, a reading every minute. On Priya's laptop, all five come from a seeded generator, so every number in this course can be produced again exactly. The terminal counts what it wrote. Five thousand households. Over three thousand charges across the last three days. A hundred and four titles. Seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty telemetry readings, one per exchange per minute. And just over four hundred thousand viewing events for one Saturday, derby day. The side pane sorts the sources into the platform's two paths. The C R M, billing and the vendor files change slowly and need to be right, so they travel as a nightly batch, answered next morning. Viewing and telemetry matter while the match is on, so they travel as a live stream, answered in seconds. Next, a closer look at the C R M.

The C R M is a PostgreSQL database, and here it runs for real. The editor shows its schema. Packages are Sun's four television bundles with a monthly price. Households hold who the customer is, including an email and a phone number, the region, and the broadband exchange that serves them. Subscriptions join the two, and the highlighted columns are the important part: a valid from date and a valid to date. A household never has its package overwritten. An upgrade closes the old row and opens a new one. In the terminal, the load script fills both the C R M and billing from the generator's files. The first query counts households by their current package: Entertainment is the most common, then Essentials, Sports and Ultimate, five thousand households in all. The second query asks for every version of one household, H H one zero zero four two. It was on Entertainment until the fifteenth of October, then switched to Sports, and that second row has no end date, so it is current. The side pane draws the tables and how they relate. One household has many subscription versions, and each version points at one package. Below, the two versions of that household and the package mix. This history matters later, when Silver has to answer which package a household had on any given night. Next, the files the vendors send.

Two of Sun's sources aren't databases at all: they are files that vendors deliver every day. The catalogue is a C S V file, one row per title, with an i d, a name, a kind and a running time. The E P G, the electronic programme guide, is a J S O N file listing every channel's slots for the day, each slot pointing at a title i d. Neither file is useful alone, so the new script, slots dot p y, joins them: for one channel and a stretch of the evening, it prints each slot with its title's name. It also does one more thing, highlighted at the bottom: when one slot ends and the next does not start straight away, it prints the hole. In the terminal, the catalogue's header and first rows. On SUN SPORTS ONE the evening reads cleanly: Sun News until half past five, then Northbridge versus Eastfield, the derby, from five thirty to seven twenty five, then live football. On SUN MOVIES TWO, two films, and then from eight to ten o'clock, no slot at all. The boxes were showing a film during those two hours, but the feed never said which. The side pane draws the join. A slot plus a title i d gives a title name. A missing slot gives nothing, and any viewing joined to the guide in those hours will find no match. Nothing fails here. The gap only matters once someone counts minutes by title, and we'll meet it again in Course eight. Next, the busiest source: one box's night of events.

Viewing events are the biggest source by far, so it's worth following one box through the derby, event by event. The editor holds a short j q filter. It picks one device's events on the sports channel that evening and prints each event as a row: the time on the box's clock, the event type, the title, the seconds watched and the milliseconds spent buffering. The comments describe the four kinds of event. A box sends play when the picture starts, a heartbeat every minute it keeps playing, buffer when the picture stalls, and stop at the end. The terminal runs it for set-top box one three seven nine five, which is served by exchange L D N zero four. Counting the event types gives one play, one hundred and thirty six heartbeats, forty buffer events and one stop. The trace itself is folded to its turning points. The box starts at ten past five, during the build-up on Sun News. At half past five the heartbeats' title changes to the derby. For the whole first half, buffering stays at zero. Then, from twenty five to seven, the stalls begin, and they keep coming until the final whistle. About five minutes of the second half went on buffering. The side pane draws this box's night, and the fields every event carries. Note that each event's time comes from the box's own clock, which is not always right. That distinction comes back when we count viewers live. Next, Google Cloud itself: signing in, and finding out what the project holds.

From here on the commands run against a real Google Cloud project, recorded once, with its real identifiers replaced, and the label at the top of the side pane says so. Before building anything, it's worth knowing three things: who is signed in, which project the commands will touch, and what already exists there. The editor holds a small file Priya sources in every Google Cloud shell. It asks g cloud for the current project and the signed in account, and hands both to Terraform as variables, so no project i d is ever typed into the code. In the terminal, the first command names the account every call will be made as. The second shows the project, sun media dev. The third asks whether the Cloud Storage A P I is switched on. In Google Cloud, every service is an A P I that each project enables separately, and Storage is already on. The last command looks for anything carrying the label app equals viewing pulse, and finds nothing: the project holds none of the platform yet. The side pane draws that chain from identity to project to enabled A P I, ending at an empty search. The table below lists the three labels Terraform will attach to every resource it makes. App says whose it is, env says which copy, and owner says who to ask. Labels are how a shared project gets filtered down to one team's resources. Next, the first resource, written as code.

Every resource in this platform is created by Terraform, never by hand, so the first bucket is a short file of code. The editor shows main dot t f. The top pins the Google provider to an exact version and sets default labels, so everything this code creates is tagged app, env and owner. The highlighted block is the raw zone's bucket. Its name is built from the project i d, because bucket names are global across all of Google Cloud. It lives in europe west two, London, uses the Standard storage class, and has two safety settings switched on: uniform bucket level access, so permissions are only ever granted on the whole bucket, and public access prevention, so nothing in it can be made public. In the terminal, terraform init downloads the pinned provider. Then terraform apply plans one resource to add, shows it, and creates it in a few seconds. The last command reads the bucket back with g cloud: its name, its location, and its labels, including one Terraform adds by itself to mark what it provisioned. The side pane follows the path of that apply. Code goes to the provider, the provider calls the Cloud Storage A P I, the same one g cloud uses, and the bucket exists. One thing in this run is still fragile. Terraform remembers what it made in a state file, and right now that file sits on Priya's laptop. Next, the state moves to Google Cloud.

Terraform keeps a state file: its record of what it created and each resource's real i d. On one laptop that file can be lost, and two people running Terraform at once would each work from their own copy. So the state moves into Cloud Storage. The editor shows the new backend file. It says the state lives in a G C S bucket, under a prefix for this environment, env slash dev. The bucket's name is passed in when Terraform starts, because a backend block can't read variables. That bucket has to exist before Terraform can use it, so it's the one thing in the whole platform made with the command line: the bootstrap script creates it, with versioning on, so every earlier state is kept. In the terminal, the script creates the state bucket. Terraform init then migrates: it takes the lock, copies the state into the bucket, and releases the lock. Listing the bucket shows one object, default dot t f state, under env slash dev. The old local files are still on the laptop, and the table in the side pane marks them as copies to delete. The final plan reads the state from the bucket, refreshes the raw bucket, and finds no changes. Notice the plan also takes the lock first. While one run holds it, a second run is refused instead of both writing the state at once. Next, the code grows into modules, and the project gets a budget.

Two things change in this step: the code gets a structure that can grow, and the project gets a budget before it costs anything. The raw bucket moves into a module, a folder of Terraform with its own inputs, and a moved block tells Terraform it's the same bucket under a new address, not a new one to create. The editor shows the budget file. A budget of fifty pounds a month, for this project only, with two threshold rules at eighty percent: one on money already spent, one on the month's forecast. Below them, outside the folded view, every alert is routed to a Monitoring email channel for the media data team. A Google Cloud budget never stops anything. It only warns. In the terminal, terraform fmt checks the formatting before anything touches the cloud, and the code is validated too. Then the apply. The plan reports the bucket moved into the module, and four resources to add: the two A P Is the budget needs, the email channel, and the budget itself, created on the billing account in about a second. The side pane draws both parts. On the left, the root file calling the storage module. Below, the budget, its eighty percent rule, and where the email goes. With the sources known, the code in place and spending watched, the next course turns to identity: who, and what, is allowed to touch any of this.

Every request to Google Cloud is checked against an allow policy, and before granting anything new it's worth reading the one the project already has. The editor shows the shell file again, because its last line matters now: Terraform runs as Priya's signed in identity, and that identity is what every policy decides about. In the terminal, the project's policy is saved as J S O N, and three small queries read it. It holds sixteen bindings. A binding is the unit of I A M: one role, and the list of members who hold it. The editor role, for example, is held by two members, and both are Google's own service agents, accounts Google Cloud creates to run services on this project's behalf. The owner role has two members. Owner can do anything in the project, including granting itself more. The side pane draws the shape. One policy is attached to the project, a binding names a role, and the role lists its members. The tables repeat the editor's two members and the owner count. Notice what's missing: nothing here says which bucket or which secret. A role granted on a project applies to everything in it. That's convenient, and it's also why the platform's own jobs will get their roles on the narrowest resource instead. Next, how a policy on a project reaches a bucket inside it.

Policies in Google Cloud stack. A resource has its own policy, and it also inherits every policy above it in the hierarchy: its project, any folders, and the organization. What a caller may do is the union of all of them, and an inherited grant can't be taken away lower down. This project sits alone, with no organization or folders, so there are two levels to read. The editor shows the raw bucket's code, and the highlighted line, uniform bucket level access, means this bucket is governed by I A M policies only, no per-object permissions. In the terminal, the project's sixteen bindings are counted, then the bucket's own policy is read. It has four bindings of its own, and none of them names a person. Their members are projectOwner, projectEditor and projectViewer: convenience bindings that Cloud Storage adds to every new bucket, pointing back up at whoever holds those roles on the project. Owners and editors get the legacy bucket owner and object owner roles. Viewers get the readers. The side pane draws the hierarchy, top to bottom. The organization level is greyed out because it doesn't exist here. The project's bindings flow down to the bucket. The bucket adds its own. The bottom card is the rule: the effective permission is the union, never less. So the way to give a job narrow access is not to subtract anything: it's to leave the job out of the project policy and grant it on the bucket alone. Next, the jobs get identities of their own.

A pipeline shouldn't run as a person. When it does, it can do everything that person can, and its actions are logged under their name. Google Cloud's answer is the service account: an identity for a program. The new I A M module creates five of them, one per job, and the editor shows the list. S A ingest lands the nightly extracts. S A dataflow runs the live viewer count. S A dataproc runs the quality of service join. S A airflow runs the nightly D A G. And S A C I C D plans and deploys from continuous integration. Each one gets a description saying who wears it, and Terraform creates them all from that one map. In the terminal, the plan has five resources to add, the apply creates them in about twelve seconds each, and listing Terraform's state shows the five accounts, now tracked like any other resource. The side pane's table lists each account and the job that runs as it. Below, the idea in one line: the nightly extract is a program, it runs as S A ingest, and S A ingest is its identity on Google Cloud. The arrow to the raw zone is dashed and the zone is greyed out, because an account starts with no permissions at all. Creating an identity grants nothing. That comes later, role by role. First, though, someone has to be able to act as these accounts, and that should never mean a key file. Next, impersonation.

The usual way to use a service account from a laptop is to download a key file for it, a long lived credential that works for anyone holding a copy. It ends up in downloads folders, in chat messages and in git history. This platform never creates one. Instead, Priya is allowed to act as each account when she needs to. The highlighted block in the I A M module grants her the service account token creator role on all five accounts. That role lets one identity ask Google for a short lived access token belonging to another. In the terminal, the apply adds those five grants. Then the last command lists S A ingest's user managed keys, the kind you can download, and there are none. Listed zero items. The side pane draws how it works instead. Priya holds the token creator grant. When she asks to act as S A ingest, Google's I A M credentials A P I checks that grant and mints an access token for the account. The token expires within the hour, so a copy that leaks stops working on its own. The table below records the key list: empty, so there is no key file to lose. In an organization, a policy can go further and refuse key creation outright. This project has no organization, so that guard isn't shown here. Next, impersonation in use, and the first refusal.

This is a step that fails on purpose, run once and then set aside. Priya acts as S A ingest and asks for something it can't do yet. The editor shows the raw bucket's code, and there's nothing in it for this account: no binding names S A ingest. In the terminal, the first command proves the impersonation works. A token is minted for the account, and only its length is printed, over a thousand characters. Then, as S A ingest, g cloud lists the raw zone, and Google refuses. The error is precise: S A ingest does not have storage dot objects dot list access to the bucket, permission denied. It even names the identity that asked and the one it impersonated. The side pane tells the story in three steps. The token works. The call needs one specific permission, storage objects list, on the raw bucket. No binding grants it, so the answer is permission denied. This is the normal shape of an I A M failure, and the way to read it: find the permission named in the error, then the narrowest role that holds it. The table maps that out. Listing objects comes with the object viewer role. Creating them comes with object creator. And deleting them comes with a role nobody on this platform will get. Both grants go on the bucket, not the project, in the last section of this course. Next, the first secret.

The nightly extract needs the C R M's database password, and that password must not live in the code, in a config file, or on anyone's laptop. Secret Manager holds it. The new secrets module does three things, and the editor highlights them. Terraform generates the password itself, thirty two random characters that nobody ever types. It stores them as the first version of a secret called C R M D B password, replicated in London only. And it grants exactly one identity the secret accessor role: S A ingest. In the terminal, the apply creates five resources. Listing the secret's versions shows version one, enabled. Then the two reads. Acting as S A ingest, the latest version is read and only its length is counted: thirty two characters, the value itself never printed. Acting as S A dataflow, the same request is refused with permission denied, because that account has no reason to know the C R M's password. The side pane draws the secret, its one version, and the two readers: S A ingest allowed, S A dataflow refused. The card at the bottom records the rule. At run time the extract will read the password as S A ingest and hold it only in memory, and rotating it later means adding a new version, not editing any code. Next, the raw zone gets Sun's own encryption key.

Everything in Cloud Storage is already encrypted, with keys Google manages. Some data, like a C R M extract full of names and phone numbers, is better encrypted with a key the company controls: it can rotate it, audit its use, and switch it off. That is a customer managed encryption key, and Cloud K M S holds it. The editor shows the K M S module. A key ring called K R media, in London. A comment warns that a key ring can never be deleted, ever, which matters for tearing a project down. Inside it, a key called K raw, rotating every ninety days. The highlighted grant is the subtle part. The bucket doesn't encrypt anything itself: Cloud Storage's own service agent does, so that agent gets the encrypter decrypter role on this one key. In the terminal, the apply creates the K M S A P I, the ring, the key and the grant, then changes the raw bucket in place, setting K raw as its default key. Describing the bucket confirms its default key. The side pane draws the chain: ring, key, version, bucket. Every new object is encrypted with the key's current version. When it rotates, new objects get the new version, and old ones stay readable. The table names who encrypts, and with what. Next, every job account gets the roles it needs, and nothing more.

With identities in place, each job gets the narrowest roles its work needs, on the narrowest resource that holds them. The editor shows the storage module's grants on the raw bucket. S A ingest gets object creator, to land files, and object viewer, so the landing gate can read them back. S A dataproc gets object viewer, to read the zone for the quality of service join. Nobody gets a role that can delete or replace an object. On the project, the processing accounts get the worker roles their services require: Dataflow worker, Dataproc worker and Composer worker. In the terminal, the apply adds six grants. Then roles dot sh reads the result back from Google, for the five job accounts only, project and bucket. It's the same matrix the code describes, now as Google holds it. Finally, acting as S A ingest, the raw zone is listed again, the request that was refused two sections ago, and this time it's allowed. The side pane's table is that matrix: each account, the resource, the role. Below, the one grant that fixed the earlier failure, on the bucket and not on the project. That's the end of identity: five accounts, no key files, one secret, Sun's own key, and a written role matrix. The next course goes back to the raw zone, now protected, and builds a nightly batch that can be trusted.

The raw zone is where each night's extracts will land, exactly as received, and after two courses of work it already exists as one Cloud Storage bucket. Before putting anything in it, it's worth reading it back the way Google sees it. The editor shows the storage module. The bucket lives in one region, London. Its storage class is Standard, the class for data that's read often. Uniform bucket level access means permissions are granted with I A M on the whole bucket, never object by object. And every new object is encrypted with Sun's own key, from the previous course. In the terminal, describing the bucket returns its real settings: the default key, the Standard class, the location, public access prevention enforced, uniform access on. The table in the side pane reads those values back and says what each one means. One line comes from Google, not from our code: soft delete, seven days, so a deleted object can still be restored for a week. Below the table is the idea the rest of this course depends on. A bucket holds objects, and nothing else. There are no folders inside it. An object called source equals billing, slash d t equals the thirty first, slash charges dot C S V is one object with one long name. The slashes are just characters in that name. Next, on Priya's laptop, those names become a partitioning scheme.

Every night, four sources arrive in Sun's raw zone, and each one needs an address that says what it is and which night it belongs to. On Priya's laptop the raw zone is fake G C S server, Cloud Storage's emulator, and the label at the top of the side pane says so. The new file is raw dot p y. Its docstring holds the idea of the whole section: Cloud Storage has no folders. An object has one flat name, and that name may contain slashes. The partition function builds the start of every name: source equals the system, then d t equals the night. The first two commands land the vendors' files for derby day, the content catalogue and the E P G, the programme guide. Then the terminal lists the same two objects three ways. With two stars, gcloud prints every whole name, slashes and all. With the bucket alone, it groups the names at the first slash and shows what look like folders; the tool made those up. With a wildcard for the source and a fixed date, it lists one night across every source, because a shared prefix is a filter. The table in the side pane splits one real name into its parts. The bucket, then source equals E P G, then d t equals the thirty first of October, then the file. In Course eight, BigQuery will read those two prefixes back as two columns, source and d t, and skip every night a query does not ask for. Next, the source systems themselves: two nightly extracts, shaped two different ways.

Sun's C R M and its billing system are PostgreSQL databases, running here for real, and each night their data has to reach the raw zone. Extract dot p y copies them, and the top of the editor declares the two shapes an extract can take. The C R M is a snapshot: households, subscriptions and packages are small enough to copy whole, every night. Billing is incremental: it posts charges all day, so each night copies only the charges updated inside that night's window, after midnight and up to the next midnight. The highlighted where clause is that window, and getting its two boundaries right is most of the work. Both extracts stream the rows out of PostgreSQL as C S V, upload one file per table under the night's partition, and finish by writing an empty object called underscore success, which says the night is complete. The terminal runs both for the thirtieth of October, the night before the derby. The C R M lands five thousand households, five thousand and one subscription versions and four packages. Billing prints its window, then lands one thousand and fifty one charges. The last command lists every marker in the raw zone: both folders are closed. The side pane draws the two paths: the C R M copied whole, billing copied by window. The table repeats the counts and says which rows each file holds. One thing in this code is too trusting. The marker is written whatever the copy delivered, and nothing checks that the copy was complete. Next, before copying the derby night, we write down what the copy is supposed to deliver.

Derby day has happened in the source systems: thirty seven households bought Sports before kick off, and billing posted the day's rentals and subscription charges. Before copying any of it, the extract now writes down what the copy must deliver. Extract dot p y has split into two steps, plan and copy, and the editor shows plan. It runs the same queries the copy will run, but only to count rows and read column names, and it writes the answer as a small J S O N object called underscore manifest, into the night's folder, first. The terminal runs plan for billing on the thirty first of October. The window runs from midnight on the thirty first to midnight on the first of November, and the charges file is expected to hold one thousand and sixty eight rows. The listing shows the order on disk: last night's folder, complete, and tonight's, holding only the manifest. The side pane shows the manifest itself, read back from the raw zone: the source, the night, each file with its expected rows, each file's eight columns in order, and the window. Above it, the order of the whole night. Plan counts, the manifest is written, then the copy writes the file, and a gate will hold the folder to the promise. Writing the promise first matters, because a copy can only report what it found. If it comes up short, it has no way of knowing, unless something wrote down beforehand what complete looks like. Next, the copy runs, and comes up short.

This is a night that goes wrong, run once and then thrown away, so the course carries on from the manifest. The new file is g one dot p y, the landing gate. It reads the manifest, lists the night's folder, and checks three things: every promised file is there, its columns are the declared ones in order, and its rows add up to the expected count. Each check prints what it found against what was promised. Only when all of them match does the gate publish the night, by writing the underscore success marker. The copy no longer writes that marker itself. In the terminal, the copy lands one thousand and sixty five rows. G one compares: one file of one, eight columns of eight, and one thousand and sixty five rows of one thousand and sixty eight. Fail. The night is not published, and asking for the last published night still answers the thirtieth of October. The last command shows why: the newest change in billing is stamped four seconds past two in the morning, after the window closed. The side pane tells the story in order. At two o'clock, plan counted one thousand and sixty eight charges. Four seconds later, billing's own job re-rated three of the night's rentals, and their updated time moved past the window's end, out of tonight's copy. Nothing crashed and no error was raised. Without the gate, a short night would have flowed on to BigQuery and into the morning's numbers. Next, on Google Cloud itself: making a rerun safe, and sealing a night so nothing can overwrite it.

Back on the real raw zone, the night is copied again, this time from a clean state with no late re-rating, and two new rules make the copy safe to repeat. A retried copy rewrites the same object names, so running it twice can never leave two versions of the night side by side. And once the landing gate passes, the night is sealed. The editor shows the seal. G one writes the underscore success marker with if generation match equals zero, a Cloud Storage precondition that means: create this object only if it does not already exist. If two runs race, exactly one seal wins. In the terminal, plan has already written the manifest, expecting one thousand and sixty eight charges. The copy lands them. The same copy again lands the same rows under the same name. G one checks the folder against the manifest, one thousand and sixty eight of one thousand and sixty eight, passes, and publishes the night. Running G one a second time passes its checks again, but the seal is refused: already sealed. And a copy after that is refused before it reads anything, because the night is sealed. The side pane follows the night down: copy and copy again, then the seal, then the two refusals side by side. The table lists the finished folder, and which step wrote each object. A sealed night is final for this pipeline. But only by its own rules: anyone with delete rights could still remove an object. Next, the bucket enforces it.

The seal stops this pipeline from rewriting a night, but it can't stop a person, a script or a wrong command from deleting one. A retention policy can. It's set on the bucket, and it applies to every object in it, whoever asks. The editor shows the new block in the storage module. Each object must reach a minimum age before it can be deleted or replaced. In this development project the age is one hour, so a recording can be torn down the same day. A production raw zone would hold its nights for years. In the terminal, the apply updates the bucket in place, and describing it shows the policy: a retention period of three thousand six hundred seconds. Then one object is chosen, the night's charges file, and Cloud Storage reports its own retention expiry, an hour after it was created. Finally, the delete. G cloud tries to remove the object and the task fails. The refusal comes from the bucket's policy. It isn't about I A M: the account asking is the project's owner. The side pane follows that chain: the object, the policy, the object's own expiry time, and the refused delete. The card at the bottom records the limit. This policy is unlocked, so it can still be shortened or removed. Locking it makes it permanent, even for the owner, and that isn't done in a course project. Next, the last rule for the raw zone: what happens as nights get old.

A night in the raw zone is read hard for a few days: by the landing gate, by the loaders, by anyone checking a number. After a month it's rarely touched, and after a year almost never, yet it must be kept. Cloud Storage has cheaper storage classes for exactly that, and lifecycle rules move objects between them by age, without anyone touching a file. The editor shows the rules, written once as a small map and expanded by Terraform. At thirty days an object moves to Nearline, at ninety to Coldline, at three hundred and sixty five to Archive. In the terminal, the apply updates the bucket in place. Describing its lifecycle configuration returns the three rules as Google stored them, each a set storage class action with an age condition: Archive, Coldline and Nearline. The side pane follows one object through its life. It lands in Standard on day zero, while the gate and the loaders read it. At thirty days it moves to Nearline, at ninety to Coldline, and after a year to Archive, where it's kept and almost never read. The card at the bottom says what each move trades. Every colder class lowers the price of keeping an object and raises the price of reading it. Together with the retention policy, a night now lands once, is sealed by the gate, can't be deleted early, and costs less every month it is kept. With the raw zone settled, the next course turns to the platform's other clock: the live stream.

The last course built a nightly batch that can be trusted. It extracts at two in the morning and is correct by breakfast. During the derby, though, nobody at Sun can wait until breakfast. The curve on the left is the answer the live lane has to draw: households watching the match, minute by minute, rising from kick off, dipping at half time and peaking in the second half. It was computed in the first course, after the fact, from every event at once. Drawn live, each point has to appear within seconds of the minute it describes. The batch can't do that. At half time it hasn't even started. On the right, the two clocks side by side. The nightly batch: extracts at two, correct by morning, no use at half time. The stream: each box's event, seconds after it happens. Between the boxes and anything that counts them sits Pub Sub, Google Cloud's messaging service. It accepts every message a publisher sends, keeps it, and hands it to every reader that has subscribed. It holds on to each message until that reader acknowledges it. This is a concept frame, and the label cites Google's Pub Sub overview. Pub Sub doesn't count anything itself. It makes sure no box's message is lost while the counting happens somewhere else, in the next course. Next, the topics and subscriptions, written in Terraform.

Pub Sub has two kinds of resource, and the new Terraform module creates both. A topic is where publishers send messages. A subscription is a reader's own queue on a topic, and every subscription gets its own copy of every message. The editor shows the module. Three topics, one for each kind of message: viewing events, network telemetry and device events. Each keeps its messages for a day, so a night can be replayed. A fourth topic, dead letter, is for messages nobody can read. Then Dataflow's subscriptions, one per topic, with two settings that matter. The acknowledgement deadline is twenty seconds: a reader that takes a message must confirm it within that time, or it's delivered again. And the dead letter policy: after five failed deliveries, a message is moved aside instead of being retried forever. In the terminal, the apply adds thirteen resources: the A P I, the four topics, the four subscriptions, and the grants that let Pub Sub's own service agent move dead letters. The two listings, filtered to this platform's label, show the topics and the subscriptions. The side pane draws the fan out. The boxes publish to topics. The table below lists each subscription and who reads it: Dataflow in the next course, and a person for the dead letters. Next, the boxes publish, on Priya's laptop.

To work on the stream without waiting for a real Saturday, the producer replays derby night into Pub Sub, as the boxes sent it. On Priya's laptop, Pub Sub is the emulator that ships with g cloud, and the label says so. The file is settop dot p y. It reads the night's events, waits until each event's moment arrives, sixty times faster than real time, and publishes it to the viewing events topic. Each message carries the event itself, as J S O N, and two attributes, the event type and the device, which a subscriber can read without opening the body. One more line is highlighted on purpose. Every four hundredth event is published twice, the way a network retry sends the same thing again. Pub Sub has no way to know the two are the same event. In the terminal, five minutes from half past five are replayed: just over ten thousand events, mostly heartbeats, with a few hundred buffers, plays and stops. The producer published ten thousand four hundred and seven messages, twenty five of them re sent by a retry. Pulling three back shows their message numbers, types, devices and event times. The side pane draws a box's event becoming a message, data plus attributes, on its way to the topic, and the table counts the replay. Next, what reading a message, and acknowledging it, actually means.

Pub Sub hands a message to a reader on loan. The reader has until the acknowledgement deadline to say it was handled. If it doesn't, the message is delivered again. That rule is what makes losing a message so hard, and this lab watches it happen. The editor shows the subscriber. It pulls up to a given number of messages, prints each one, and acknowledges them all, unless told not to. In the terminal, three of one box's heartbeats are published. The first pull takes two and acknowledges them. The second pull takes the third, message three, and doesn't acknowledge it, as if the reader had crashed. The terminal then waits twelve seconds, longer than this subscription's ten second deadline. The last pull asks for up to five messages and gets exactly one: message three again, the same message number and the same event. This time it's acknowledged, and it won't come back. The side pane follows message three: pulled and leased for ten seconds, never acknowledged, and delivered again once the lease ran out. The table lists every message the three pulls returned, with message three appearing twice. So Pub Sub keeps a message until someone acknowledges it. The flip side follows directly. A message can arrive more than once, and a reader has to be ready for that. Next, duplicates on purpose.

Pub Sub promises that every message is delivered at least once. It doesn't promise exactly once, and the replay's retries make that visible. The editor shows a counter. It drains a subscription, acknowledging everything, and counts two things separately: message numbers, which Pub Sub gives every message it accepts, and event i ds, which the box gave the event. In the terminal, five minutes from half past six are published, and the producer reports twenty three retries. The counter drained nine thousand two hundred and fifty five messages, but only nine thousand two hundred and thirty two distinct events. Twenty three events arrived twice, as two different messages carrying the same event i d, and one is printed as an example. Nothing failed here. Each copy was a valid message, delivered and acknowledged once. The duplication happened before Pub Sub, at the publisher, and from Pub Sub's point of view there are simply two messages. The side pane's table lays out the three counts. Below it, who removes the second copy. Pub Sub doesn't. The Dataflow job will drop repeated event i ds inside each counting window, so the live curve isn't inflated. And next morning, Silver keeps exactly one row per event i d, whatever arrived. Counting messages instead of events would have overstated the derby. Next, keeping one device's events in order.

Pub Sub delivers messages in parallel, and by default in no particular order. That's how it scales. For a single device, though, order can matter: a stop that arrives before its play makes a confusing session. Ordering keys give one lane to each key. The highlighted lines turn ordering on in the publisher, and give every message an ordering key, the device i d. On the reading side, the subscription viewing events ordered has message ordering switched on. Together they guarantee that messages with the same key are delivered in the order they were published, while messages with different keys still flow in parallel. In the terminal, eight minutes of box one three seven nine five are published with ordering on: fifteen events, buffers and heartbeats from its stalling second half. The ordered subscription returns all fifteen, in publish order: a buffer, the heartbeat that follows it, the next buffer, and so on, minute by minute. The side pane draws the lane. The ordering key is the device. The ordered subscription preserves the key's order, and the table shows the first eight messages as they arrived. One limit is worth stating. An ordering key preserves the order in which messages were published. A box that sends late, or with a wrong clock, still publishes out of event time order, and that's a problem for the counting itself, in the next course. Next, the message nobody can read.

Sooner or later something publishes a message no reader can understand. If the reader refuses it, Pub Sub delivers it again, and again, forever, and it blocks nothing else but wastes everything. The dead letter policy from this course's Terraform puts a limit on that. This was recorded on Google Cloud. The editor shows a strict subscriber. Anything that isn't valid J S O N, it refuses with a negative acknowledgement, a nack, and it prints which delivery attempt it was. In the terminal, a broken message is published to viewing events: a J S O N object cut off halfway. The strict subscriber watches for seventy five seconds. Attempt one, not J S O N, nack. Attempts two, three and four the same, ten seconds apart, the subscription's retry policy. Attempt five, nack, and then nothing: the subscription has given up on it. The last command pulls from dead letter audit, and there it is. The broken body, plus attributes Pub Sub added when it moved the message: the delivery count, five, the subscription and project it came from, and when it was first published. The side pane draws that path: a poison message, five deliveries, the dead letter topic, and a person reading it with its history attached. The table lists those attributes. With every box's events arriving and nothing lost, the next course counts viewers while the match plays.

Dataflow runs programs written with Apache Beam, so the first step is Beam's model itself, shown here with the smallest pipeline that does anything. The file is hello dot p y. It starts from six event kinds and turns them into a P Collection, Beam's name for a set of elements flowing through a pipeline. A Map transform turns each kind into a pair: the kind, and the number one. A Combine Per Key transform then brings together every pair with the same key and adds them up. Each step is a P Transform, and each one produces a new P Collection. Nothing changes in place. In the terminal, it prints the totals: one buffer, three heartbeats, one play and one stop. The side pane draws the same thing as a graph: a P Collection, two transforms, a P Collection out. Map works on each element independently, so its work can be split across any number of machines. Combine Per Key needs every element with the same key brought together first, and that grouping is the expensive part on a real cluster. The card at the bottom holds the most useful idea in Beam. The pipeline doesn't say where it runs. The table names two runners. The DirectRunner runs it on this laptop, which is where the rest of this course works. The DataflowRunner hands the identical graph to Google's workers, in the last section. Next, a first real pipeline over derby night's events.

The first real pipeline reads derby night's events and counts them, the simplest useful question to ask of the stream. The file is live viewers dot p y, and it will grow through this whole course. Right now the highlighted lines are a straight chain. Read the night's events, one line each. Parse each line from J S O N into an event. Keep only the events in a five minute slice, here half past six to twenty five to seven. Pair each event with its type, and count per type. In the terminal, five minutes of the derby come out as eight and a half thousand heartbeats, five hundred and ten buffer events, a hundred and eighty two plays and eight stops. Almost everything is heartbeats, as expected for a match with households settled in. The side pane draws the pipeline graph, read, parse, keep the slice, count, with the counts in the table below. One step hides a problem. The slice is a filter on each event's timestamp, so the pipeline has to see every event before it can be sure it has them all. That's fine for a file that already holds the whole night. It doesn't work for a stream, where events are still arriving and some arrive late. A stream needs a different idea of time. Next, the two clocks every event has.

Every event carries two times. Event time is when the box says something happened. Processing time is when the platform actually hears about it. Usually they're seconds apart. Not always. The file arrivals dot p y models how derby night's events arrived, and it plants a known fault. Most boxes are heard one to four seconds after the event. One device in every thirty seven is slow, because of a clock that runs minutes behind or a connection that buffers, and is heard four to six minutes late. It also re sends one event in every four hundred, as the producer did in the last course. It's deterministic: the same night always arrives the same way. In the terminal, the sports channel from eighteen thirty eight, six minutes of it: just over fourteen thousand deliveries, from forty six slow boxes. The first rows show three late ones: events from eighteen thirty eight, heard at eighteen forty two, about four and a half minutes late. The next three show normal boxes, heard within a second. The side pane plots event time against processing time. The diagonal line is on time. Most dots would sit on it, while the slow boxes sit well above it. The table repeats the six rows. So if a pipeline counts by the time it hears an event, a slow box's viewing lands in the wrong minute. Next, counting by event time, in windows.

To count viewers per minute, the pipeline has to know which minute each event belongs to, by event time, not by when it was heard. Beam does this in two steps, and both are highlighted. First, every event is stamped with its event time, taken from the box's own timestamp. Then the stamped events are placed into fixed windows, sixty seconds each, back to back. From there, every grouping and counting step works within one window at a time. Inside each window, the pipeline pairs the channel with the household and keeps each pair once, so a household with many heartbeats in a minute counts once. Then it counts per channel. In the terminal, six minutes of the sports channel. Eighteen thirty eight has just over two thousand and sixty households. Then two thousand one hundred and thirty nine at every minute from eighteen thirty nine, except eighteen forty one, which has two thousand one hundred and forty: the derby's peak, the same number the first course computed. The side pane plots the six windows as bars, with the counts in the table. These numbers are correct because the whole night was already in the file. In a live stream, the pipeline has to decide when a minute is finished. The slow boxes are still four minutes behind, so if it decides too early, it undercounts. Next, the watermark: how a stream decides.

A stream never knows for certain that a minute is finished, because a slow box might still be sending. Beam's answer has two parts, and this pipeline shows both. The file late dot p y feeds the events in the order they were heard, each stamped with its event time. Alongside them it advances a watermark: the pipeline's running estimate that nothing older than a given time is still on its way. Here the watermark trails what has been heard by ten seconds. The highlighted trigger says when to emit a count. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the window fires on time. Each late event that arrives afterwards fires it again, and the counts accumulate. Allowed lateness keeps the window open for ten minutes past its end. In the terminal are two windows. Eighteen forty fired on time with two thousand and ninety three households, then received fifty three late panes, ending at two thousand one hundred and thirty nine. Eighteen forty one fired on time with two thousand and ninety four. Fifty two late panes followed, each a slow box heard minutes after the fact, and it ended at two thousand one hundred and forty, the true peak. The side pane follows the eighteen forty one window through all of that, and the table lists both windows. A live chart can show the on time number at once and correct it as late data arrives. Next, the retries' second copies.

The last course showed Pub Sub delivering some events twice. Counting households hides the problem, because a household counts once a minute however many copies arrive. Adding up seconds watched doesn't hide it. A duplicate heartbeat adds sixty seconds that nobody watched. The pipeline now reads the events as they were delivered, retries included, and counts each minute twice: once as delivered, and once after dropping the duplicates. The highlighted lines do the dropping. Inside each window, every event is keyed by its event i d. Grouping brings a retry next to its first copy, and only one is kept. Only then are the seconds added up. In the terminal, the same six minutes. The household counts are unchanged, as expected. Seconds watched, though, are higher as delivered, by three hundred seconds in most minutes and three hundred and sixty in some: five or six duplicate heartbeats per minute. The table in the side pane lists all six minutes, and every row where the two disagree is marked. Below, the three steps of the dedupe: events arrive keyed by event i d, grouping puts copies together, one is kept. Dedupe happens inside the window because that's where the copies meet. A retry arrives seconds after its first copy, so the two land in the same minute. Next, a different kind of window, one that follows a household's own viewing.

Fixed windows cut time into equal slices. Some questions need a window shaped by the viewer instead, like how long someone watched before leaving. A session window does that. It grows while events keep arriving less than a gap apart, and it closes once the gap passes in silence. The file sessions dot p y applies session windows to one device's derby night, with the gap as a parameter, and counts the events in each session. In the terminal it runs three times. Box one zero zero zero two with a thirty minute gap: one session, from nine minutes past five to nineteen thirty seven, a hundred and nine events. The same box with a ten minute gap: two sessions, one ending at eighteen twenty seven and another starting at eighteen thirty nine. This household left at half time and came back twenty two minutes later. With a thirty minute gap the break disappears. With ten minutes it shows. Box one three seven nine five, which never left, stays a single session even at ten minutes. Notice each session ends one gap after its last event, because that's when the window knew it was over. The side pane plots each run as bars, one per session, with the times and counts in the table. The gap is a business decision, not a technical one, so it's stated in the code. Next, the counts go into BigQuery, on Google Cloud.

Counts printed in a terminal help nobody watching the match, so the pipeline now writes every minute into BigQuery, where a dashboard can read it. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. Terraform adds the live dataset and its table, concurrent viewers: a minute, a channel, households and seconds watched, partitioned by day, so a query reads only the nights it asks for. The editor shows the change to the pipeline. Each minute's deduplicated count becomes a row, and a new sink writes the rows to BigQuery with streaming inserts, so each one can be queried as soon as it lands. The table isn't created by the pipeline. Terraform made it, and the pipeline refuses to create one. In the terminal, the apply creates the dataset and table. The pipeline then runs over the whole derby, from half past five to half past seven. A hundred and twenty minutes go into BigQuery, ending as the audience drifts away after the final whistle. The last command queries the table with b q, with a cap on bytes billed, as every query in this course has. The top three minutes come back, led by eighteen forty one: two thousand one hundred and forty households, the derby's peak, now in a table. The side pane follows the rows from pipeline to table, and repeats the query's answer. One thing is still local: the pipeline ran on this laptop. Next, the same file on Dataflow.

Until now every pipeline ran on this laptop and finished. On Dataflow the same file becomes a job that runs on Google's workers and never finishes by itself. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. Terraform adds what the job needs: the Dataflow API, a bucket for its staged code, and grants for its own service account to read the subscription and write the live table. One grant was learned the hard way. A job that reads event time from a message attribute makes a second subscription of its own to track its watermark, and without the right to create one the job ran, read, and never closed a window. The editor shows the change that mattered most. The job's watermark follows the clock, and this is a replay of Saturday, so every event arrives days late. A live feed would keep ten minutes of lateness; the replay keeps three days, and gathers each minute's late events into a firing every thirty seconds. Because a firing repeats what came before, seconds watched are counted once per event, not added again. In the terminal the job starts, the set-top boxes replay twelve minutes of the second half into Pub/Sub, and after five minutes the job is drained. A drain stops reading, closes every open window, writes what it holds, and stops; a cancel would throw that away. The query reads back what the job wrote: each minute fired three or four times, its last firing the whole count, and eighteen forty one is the peak again: two thousand one hundred and forty households, the same answer the laptop gave. Next course, the batch: the same night, landed and cleaned in BigQuery.

The stream answers while the match is on. The batch answers next morning, and checks its answer, and that work happens in BigQuery. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. In BigQuery, tables live in datasets, and a dataset fixes two things for good: where its data is stored, and who may read it. The editor shows the module Terraform applies: one dataset per layer. Bronze holds the night as it was delivered, with a note of where every row came from. Silver holds what it means: one row per real event, in Sun's own names. Gold holds the answers the business asks for. And audit holds every gate's verdict, every night, so a number in Gold can always be traced to the checks it passed. All four sit in London, beside the raw bucket, because a query cannot join tables stored in different locations. In the terminal, the apply adds the four datasets, and b q l s lists them, with Course 7's live dataset beside them. The side pane shows the path the night will take: from Bronze, judged and deduplicated, into Silver; from Silver, into the answers. Next, the night's viewing arrives, and BigQuery reads it where it lies.

Every night the platform that runs the boxes and the app exports the day's viewing events: four files of JSON lines. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. In the terminal, the four parts are copied into the raw bucket, under source equals viewing, and a folder for the night, the same shape Course 5 gave every source. The editor shows how BigQuery reads them without loading anything. An external table is only a schema laid over files: the column names and types, the bucket path, and one more instruction. Hive partitioning reads the night's date straight out of the path, so d t becomes a column a query can filter on. In the terminal, Terraform adds the table, and a query counts the night by platform, reading the four files as it runs. Four hundred and one thousand, nine hundred and fifty eight rows came back, more than the night's events, and the platform names are the clients' own: S T B, Web, Android and i O S, not the names Sun uses. Nothing is wrong yet; this is what was delivered. The side pane shows the idea: files in the bucket, a schema over them, a query that reads them in place. Next, the night is kept in a real table, exactly as it arrived.

An external table rereads the files on every query, and the raw zone keeps them only as long as its rules say. So the night is copied once into a table of its own, Bronze, exactly as delivered. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. The editor shows the copy. It selects every column from the external table and adds two: underscore src file, the object each row was read from, which BigQuery supplies as a hidden column; and underscore ingest t s, when the copy ran. Nothing is fixed on the way in. A retry stays a retry, and a row with a missing field stays missing. Bronze is the evidence: if a number in Gold is ever questioned, the row behind it can be found, with the file it came from. In the terminal, Terraform adds the table, and the script runs with the night as a parameter. Four hundred and one thousand, nine hundred and fifty eight rows are inserted, and the count per file shows all four parts, about a hundred thousand rows each. The side pane follows a row from the files, through the insert, into Bronze with its provenance. Next, a look inside BigQuery: how it ran a query over these rows.

BigQuery has no server to size and no index to build, and it still reads a night of events in under a second. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. BigQuery keeps storage and compute apart. Tables are stored by column in Google's distributed file system, so a query reads only the columns it names. The work is done by slots, units of compute borrowed for the length of a query, connected to storage by a very fast network. The editor shows the query: each channel's busiest minute of the night, a count of distinct households per channel and minute, then the top minute per channel. In the terminal a small script runs it with a cap on bytes billed and prints the plan BigQuery made. The rows come first: SUN-SPORTS-1 peaks at eighteen forty one with two thousand one hundred and forty households, far above every other channel. Then the cost: about twelve million bytes, only the four columns the query names, and just over a second of slot time. The plan reads in stages. The input stage scans every row and passes on the ones it needs; the aggregate stages shrink them to one per channel and minute, then one per channel. The side pane shows the plan beside the machine that ran it. Next, making the same question read less.

BigQuery bills by the bytes a query reads, so the cheapest byte is the one it never touches. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. The question is the second half's busiest minute on the derby's channel. A small script asks BigQuery twice: first a dry run, which is free and only estimates, then the real query with a cap on what it may bill. Against Bronze as it stands, one undivided table, the answer is eighteen forty one with two thousand one hundred and forty households, and it reads about twelve million bytes, every row's time, channel and household. The editor shows the change. Bronze is now split into a partition per hour of event time, and inside each partition the rows are sorted by channel, then title. Partitioning is decided when a table is made, so Terraform's plan says the table must be replaced, and the apply drops it and makes it again. The night is loaded once more, and the same question reads about six and a half million bytes, roughly half. The filter names the second half, so only two hourly partitions are opened, and inside them clustering lets BigQuery skip the other channels' blocks. The dry run already knew: partitions are pruned before a query runs. The bill shows ten megabytes, BigQuery's smallest charge for a query. Next, the rows Silver should never trust.

Bronze keeps everything, including rows that would quietly corrupt an answer. Gate two decides which rows Silver may trust. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. The editor shows the judgement. Every row of the night is checked against two rules: it must carry an event I D, or it can never be deduplicated, and its title must be in the catalogue, which the vendor delivers to the raw zone and BigQuery reads in place. A row that breaks a rule gets a reason. The failing rows are copied to a quarantine table with that reason, and the gate's verdict is written to the audit dataset. G2 does not stop the night for a handful of bad rows; it passes while fewer than one row in a thousand is quarantined, because past that the delivery itself is broken. In the terminal, Terraform adds the quarantine and audit tables and the catalogue's external table. The script quarantines seven rows: four heartbeats that arrived with no event I D, a fault in one batch of firmware, and three that name T nine nine nine nine, a title Sun has never listed. The side pane shows the split: most rows go on to Silver, the seven wait in quarantine, each with its reason. Next, Silver itself.

Silver holds one row for every real event, in Sun's own words. The frame's output is mocked: the copy into Silver ran on Google Cloud, but the count after it failed, and this course now authors its terminals instead of recording them. The editor shows the copy. Every Bronze row of the night is read, except the ones gate two quarantined. A retry from the boxes is the same event I D delivered twice, so QUALIFY with ROW NUMBER keeps one row per event I D: the first copy loaded, ordered by load time, then file. The same statement renames the platforms, from what each client calls itself, S T B or i O S, to Sun's names: settop, app i o s, app android and web. In the terminal, Silver is created and filled, four hundred thousand, nine hundred and forty nine events, from four hundred and one thousand, nine hundred and fifty eight delivered rows: about a thousand retries gone, and seven rows that never made it past the gate. The next query was recorded: the derby's busiest minute, from Silver, is eighteen forty one, two thousand one hundred and forty households, the same answer the stream gave during the match. Next, the subscribers, and how their packages change over time.

A household's package changes, and the report must know which package it had on the night it watched. The frame's output is mocked: the load in the recording was refused for a missing schema, so the corrected load and the merges after it are authored to match the data. Each night's CRM snapshot is loaded into Bronze, with the night read from its path. The editor shows the merge into a slowly changing dimension, type two. Each household's current package is compared with the dimension's current row. If it is new, it is inserted. If the package changed, two things happen in one statement: the old row is closed, its valid to set to the day of the change, and a new row is opened from that day. The trick is that a changed household arrives twice in the source, once under its key to close the old row, and once with no key, so it can only be inserted. In the terminal, the thirtieth makes five thousand current rows. The thirty first, derby day, closes thirty seven, the households that bought Sports for the match, and opens thirty seven. Household ten one two three shows the result: Essentials until the thirty first, Sports from that day, and Sports is the package it had for the derby. Next, the last gate of the night.

Viewing becomes content performance only when each watched minute is tied to what was on air, and that comes from the programme guide. Gate three asks whether the guide covers every minute boxes watched a channel. This step was recorded on Google Cloud. The vendor's guide is one JSON document of channels and slots, a shape BigQuery cannot read in place, so a small loader flattens it into eighty slots in Silver. The editor shows the check. Each channel's minutes of heartbeats are joined to the slots with a left join, which keeps a minute even when no slot matches, and a minute with no title is counted. In the terminal the answer is plain. Five channels are fully covered. SUN MOVIES two loses three thousand, seven hundred and eighty one box minutes from eight o'clock, two hours the guide has no slot for. An inner join would have dropped them without a word, and the night's film audience would be quietly short. The last query reads the audit table: G2 passed with seven rows quarantined; G3 failed, a hundred and twenty channel minutes without a slot. Gold must not be built on that failure until the guide is fixed. Next course, Spark for the heaviest join of the night.

BigQuery answers most of the night's questions in S Q L. One question is heavier: joining every box's viewing to the network's own measurements, exchange by exchange, minute by minute, to see where the picture broke. That is a job for Spark, and on Google Cloud Spark runs on Dataproc. Dataproc comes in three shapes, and the difference is what is left to manage. On the left, a cluster: virtual machines that Dataproc installs Spark on. Priya chooses how many and how big, and pays while they are up, busy or idle, until she deletes them. In the middle, Dataproc Serverless: she hands over a PySpark file and its arguments, Google starts the executors that batch needs, scales them, and removes them when it ends; the bill is the compute the batch used. On the right, Dataproc on G K E, for teams that already run Kubernetes and want Spark as pods beside everything else. This frame is a concept, and its label cites Google's Dataproc overviews. viewing pulse runs one heavy batch a night, so it uses Serverless: no cluster sits idle between derbies.
