From this course on, the frames' outputs are mocked: written to match the code and the night's facts, and labelled as such. Next, the same Spark code, on this laptop first.

A Spark job is cheapest to get right on a laptop, against files, before any cluster is involved. The editor shows the heart of qos by exchange. The viewing events are read from the night's file, kept to the derby, and joined to the C R M's households to learn each one's broadband exchange. They are grouped by exchange and minute: how many households were watching, how many seconds they watched, how many seconds they spent buffering. That is what the boxes saw. Then each row is joined to the exchange's own telemetry for the same minute, its latency and packet loss: what the network measured. Spark runs here on four cores of the laptop, and its own logging is turned down so the terminal shows the result. The terminal shows two exchanges from eighteen thirty three. On E X L D N zero four, buffering jumps from about two hundred seconds a minute to seven hundred at eighteen thirty five, and latency goes from around eleven milliseconds to over eighty, with loss above one percent. On E X L D N zero one, the same minutes are calm. The boxes and the network tell the same story, independently. Next, reading the night from Silver instead of a file.

On Dataproc, the night will come from Silver, not a file, and Spark reads BigQuery through a connector. The terminal's output is mocked. The editor shows the read. The connector is a package Spark fetches on first use. The table is silver viewing events; the where clause keeps the night and the derby, and the select keeps three columns. None of that is done by Spark. The connector hands the filters and the column list to BigQuery's Storage Read API, which applies them inside BigQuery and streams back only the rows and columns asked for. The script prints what Spark's own plan says it pushed down: the filters on the night and the title, and a read schema of three columns. Two hundred and forty seven thousand, three hundred and two derby events arrive, not four hundred thousand rows of eleven columns. That is the difference between paying to move the whole night and paying to move the match. The side pane traces the request from Spark, through the read session, to the rows that come back. Next, the night's real question: how much each exchange buffered.

Minute by minute, one exchange looked bad. The report needs a single number per exchange that can be compared fairly, whatever its size. The editor shows it: over the whole derby, the seconds spent buffering divided by the seconds watched. A big exchange and a small one are measured on the same scale. The output is mocked, and matches the facts the generator planted. In the terminal, every exchange is listed, worst first. E X L D N zero four buffered forty one thousand, eight hundred and ninety five seconds for about a million seconds watched: four point one percent. Every other exchange sits at zero point six percent, the baseline of a healthy network. The side pane draws the ratio per exchange, one bar towering over eleven, and the card says what the minutes showed: almost all of zero four's buffering came after eighteen thirty five, in the second half. Before Spark can run this every night on Google Cloud, there is a problem with how the night's work is shared out. Next, the derby, as a straggler.

This is a failure step: the job is right, and slower than it needs to be. The editor shows a join of the night's events to the catalogue, by title, with Spark's adaptive execution switched off and the shuffle in eight partitions. A shuffle sends every row to a partition chosen by its key's hash, so all the rows of one title land in the same task. The terminal shows the result, and then, from Spark's own monitoring A P I, how many rows each of the eight tasks read. One task read two hundred and fifty nine thousand, six hundred and twenty three rows. The next read under thirty nine thousand. The derby is one title and sixty two percent of the night, so one task carries it, and the whole stage waits for that task while the others sit finished. On a laptop that costs seconds. On a busy night on Dataproc it costs the batch's whole schedule, and more executors don't help, because a single partition can only run on one. The side pane draws the eight tasks: one bar, and seven stubs. Next, two ways to split the derby's partition.

There are two ways to spread the derby, and the editor shows both. The first is Spark's own. Adaptive query execution watches the shuffle's real sizes, and its skew join splits any partition far larger than the rest into pieces, each joined to a copy of the other side. The thresholds are set low here, because this night is small; the defaults are sized for a real cluster. The second is salting, by hand. Each event gets a salt from zero to three, taken from its event I D, and the catalogue is copied four times, once per salt. The join key becomes the title and the salt, so one title's rows spread over four partitions. In the terminal, with adaptive execution on, the join's stage now runs eleven tasks: the derby's partition was cut in four, and the biggest task reads about a hundred thousand rows. With salting, eight tasks, the largest about ninety one thousand. The answers are identical either way. Adaptive execution needs no change to the query, so it is the first thing to reach for. Salting is for when the hot key is known and the engine can't see it. Next, the batch on Dataproc Serverless.

The laptop's answer has to run every night without the laptop. The terminal's output is mocked. Terraform adds what a Serverless batch needs: the Dataproc A P I, a network and subnet whose machines reach Google's services with no public address, a firewall rule so Spark's driver and executors can talk, a bucket for the batch's files, and grants for the batch's service account to read Silver and write Gold. The editor shows the batch's code. It reads Silver through the connector, with the night and the derby pushed down, takes households from the C R M's file in the raw zone, and computes the buffering ratio per exchange. In the terminal, a few variables hold the region, subnet, runtime and service account, and one command submits the batch. Dataproc starts a driver and executors for it, streams the driver's output back, and removes them when it finishes. The answer is the laptop's: E X L D N zero four at four point one percent, every other exchange at zero point six. The side pane shows the batch: a file and its arguments, executors started for it, Silver and the raw zone read. Next, the answer written to Gold, safely.

A nightly job will one day run twice for the same night, after a retry or a fix, and the second run must not double anything. The terminal's output is mocked. Terraform adds Gold's table for the answer: one row per exchange, partitioned by night. The editor shows the write. With the write flag, the batch saves its result to gold q o s by exchange in overwrite mode, with partition overwrite set to dynamic. Overwrite alone would replace the whole table, every night ever written. Dynamic overwrite replaces only the partitions the result contains: this night, and nothing else. In the terminal the batch runs with write, and a query counts what Gold holds: twelve exchanges for the thirty first, the worst at four point one percent. Then the same batch runs again, exactly as before, and the query returns the same twelve rows, not twenty four. That is what idempotent means for a nightly job: running it again gives the same table. The side pane shows the night's partition replaced, and every other night left alone. The heavy join is done. Next course, the answers themselves: Gold, served cheaply and safely.

Silver says what happened. Gold answers the questions the business asks every morning, and the first is simple: what did people watch last night, and how. The terminal's output is mocked, computed from the night's data the way the query would. Terraform adds Gold's table, one row per title, platform and region for each night, and an external table over the C R M's households, for their region. The editor shows how a row is made. Each heartbeat in Silver is one minute of one box. A minute on a channel is live; a minute with no channel is catch-up. The minutes are counted per title, platform and region, and so are the households watching. Households are kept twice: as a count, and as a sketch, for a reason the next section shows. The script deletes the night first and writes it again, so it can always be run again. Six hundred and one rows come out. The top titles say what anyone at Sun could guess: the derby, two hundred and twenty five thousand live minutes, far ahead of Sun News and the afternoon's football. Films and series earn a share of their minutes on catch-up. Next, a trap in counting households.

How many households watched anything last night? Gold holds a household count on every row, and adding them up is the obvious answer, and wrong. The output is mocked. The editor shows four ways to ask. Summing Gold's counts gives eight thousand, two hundred and fifty six: a household that watched three titles is counted three times. Counting distinct households in Silver gives three thousand, five hundred and seventy eight, exactly, but it reads every event of the night to do it. Approx count distinct gives the same here; it trades a small, known error, around one percent, for reading and remembering far less, which matters on a billion rows, not on this night. The fourth way uses what Gold stored: a sketch per row, a few kilobytes that summarise which households were seen. Sketches, unlike counts, can be merged, so merging them over every row of the night gives three thousand, five hundred and seventy eight without touching Silver at all. The side pane draws the idea: a sketch per row, one merge, the answer. Every dashboard that asks about households should merge sketches, never add counts. Next, a gate that checks Gold itself.

Gold is a summary, and a summary may regroup minutes but never gain or lose one. Gate four checks exactly that. This step is a failure, and its output is mocked. The editor shows a change that looks harmless: Gold gains each household's package, joined from the subscriber dimension built in Course 8. The join matches on household alone. The gate counts heartbeats in Silver, sums live and catch-up minutes in Gold, and writes its verdict to the audit table. In the terminal, Gold is rebuilt and G4 runs. Silver holds three hundred and seventy thousand and forty one minutes. Gold holds two thousand, four hundred and twenty three more. The extra minutes come from thirty seven households, the ones that bought Sports on derby day. Each has two rows in the dimension, the closed Essentials row and the current Sports row, and a join on household alone matches both, so every one of their minutes is counted twice. Nothing about Gold looks wrong to the eye: the derby still leads, the shares look sensible. Only the reconciliation shows it. The side pane follows one household's minutes into both rows of the dimension, and the fix: join to the row valid on the night. Next, the fix, and what a query costs.

First the fix: the join now takes the package valid on the night, where valid from is on or before it and valid to is after it, so each household matches one row. Gold is rebuilt and G4 passes, the same minutes in Silver and Gold. The output is mocked. Now the bill. BigQuery charges for the bytes a query reads, and three guards keep that honest. The editor shows the first, in Terraform: Silver now requires a partition filter, so any query must name the hours it wants. In the terminal, a dry run prices the dashboard's derby curve before running it: about six and a half million bytes, and the dry run itself is free. Then the same curve with the time filter forgotten, the classic mistake that scans every hour ever loaded. BigQuery refuses it outright, naming the column it wanted a filter on. Last, the cap every query in this course sets. With a cap of one megabyte, the curve is refused before it runs, and the message gives the minimum BigQuery would accept. A cap turns an expensive mistake into an error message. The side pane lists the three guards and what each did. Next, sharing Gold without sharing households.

Marketing wants to know how titles performed by region. They should never see which households watched what. The output is mocked. The editor shows the arrangement in Terraform. Marketing gets a dataset of its own, holding one view, title audience: minutes per title and region, and households merged from sketches, never a household I D. The view is then authorized on Gold: Gold's own access list names the view, so the view may read Gold's table, while the people who query the view have no access to Gold at all. Marketing's group is a reader of its own dataset, and nothing else. In the terminal, the view answers marketing's question about the derby: a thousand and eighty seven households in London, about five hundred and thirty each in the North West and the Midlands, with their minutes. Then Gold's access list is shown: the view is there, authorized, and no group appears on Gold. A query by marketing on Gold itself would be refused. The side pane draws the chain: dataset, authorized view, reader. One copy of the data, two audiences, each seeing only what it should. Next, making the dashboard's most common query nearly free.

A dashboard asks the same question all day: the derby's curve, households per minute. Scanning Silver for it each time is wasteful. The output is mocked. The editor shows two additions. A materialized view in Gold keeps the curve itself, a row per minute and channel, and BigQuery refreshes it as Silver changes, so a query reads the small stored result, plus only rows newer than the last refresh. And a BI Engine reservation of one gigabyte in London keeps hot tables in memory for dashboard queries. In the terminal, the curve is asked twice through the bytes script, which now also reports BI Engine's mode. From Silver, it reads six and a half million bytes, billed at the ten megabyte minimum, and BI Engine is not used. From the materialized view, BI Engine serves the whole query from memory: nothing read from storage, nothing billed. The side pane follows the curve from the base table, into the view, into memory. A materialized view earns its place when one query shape dominates; BI Engine when dashboards ask it often. Next, a model of the numbers themselves.

Every dashboard that counts households should merge sketches, and every one that counts minutes should read Gold's columns the same way. Writing that rule into each dashboard's S Q L is how numbers drift apart. A semantic model writes it once. This frame is a concept, and its label cites Google's Looker documentation; viewing pulse has no Looker instance, and nothing runs. On the left is a LookML view of Gold's content table. It names dimensions, title, region and the night, and measures: live minutes as a sum, and households as a merge of the stored sketches, the rule from earlier in this course, written once. Below it, an explore: the view as business users may slice it, always filtered to recent nights, so nobody scans every partition by accident. On the right, the layers. The table holds the rows. The view gives them names and rules. The explore decides what can be combined. The dashboard asks, and Looker writes the S Q L, so the derby's households are the same number in every report that shows them. Next, the answer this whole film has been building: the derby card.

On the night of the derby, Sun needed two answers: how many were watching, while it was happening, and why some of them complained. This query puts both lanes side by side. The output is mocked. The editor shows one statement reading three tables: the live lane's table, which Dataflow filled during the match; Gold's content performance, built next morning after every gate; and Gold's quality of service, from the Spark batch. In the terminal, a single row. The live lane's peak: two thousand one hundred and forty households at eighteen forty one. Gold's audience for the derby: two thousand one hundred and forty households, two hundred and twenty five thousand live minutes. The two lanes were built differently, on different clocks, and they agree. And the complaints: E X L D N zero four, one London exchange, buffered four point one percent of everything it delivered, against zero point six everywhere else, almost all of it from eighteen thirty five, the second half. The side pane is the card the business sees. The live number arrived in seconds; the batch confirmed it in the morning, checked by gates; Spark found where the picture broke. Next course, running all of it every night, and what happens when a night fails.

Everything so far was run by hand, one step at a time. Every night it has to run by itself, in order, and stop when something is wrong. That is orchestration, and on Google Cloud it is Apache Airflow, managed as Cloud Composer. This frame is a concept, and its label cites Airflow's and Composer's documentation. On the left, what Priya writes: a D A G, a graph of tasks with no cycles, one run per night. Some tasks are sensors, which wait for something outside, like the night's files. Most are operators, each one kind of work: a BigQuery job, a Dataproc batch, a shell command. And some are checks, tasks whose only job is to fail when a gate failed. On the right, what runs it. The scheduler reads the folder of D A G files, makes a run for each night, and queues a task once everything upstream of it has succeeded. Workers run the tasks and report each one's state: success, up for retry, or failed. A metadata database remembers every run and every try. Airflow does no data work itself. It decides when BigQuery and Dataproc should, and what happens when they fail. Next, the D A G for viewing pulse.

The night's work becomes one file. The terminal's output is mocked. Airflow runs on this laptop in its own environment on Python three twelve, because Composer three's image runs Airflow two point ten, which stops there. The editor shows the D A G, viewing daily. A helper turns each S Q L file from the warehouse into a BigQuery job, with the night passed in as its date parameter. Another turns each gate into a check that fails unless the gate's latest verdict passed. The last lines are the order: wait for the night, load Bronze, run G2 and its check, build Silver, load the guide, run G3 and its check, then in parallel the Spark batch and Gold, and finally G4. One change came with it. Every S Q L file now deletes its night before writing it, so a task can run again without doubling anything. In the terminal, three variables are imported: the raw bucket, the Spark job's file and its service account. The D A G parses without errors, and the tree of tasks matches the night: thirteen tasks, three of them gates. The side pane lists them in order. Next, the first task: waiting for the night to arrive.

The schedule says half past two, but the device platform's export arrives when it arrives. Loading a half-written night would be worse than loading none. The output is mocked. The editor shows the sensor. It checks for one object in the raw bucket: the night's underscore SUCCESS marker, which the exporter writes last, after every part file. It looks every five minutes for up to six hours, in reschedule mode, so between looks it gives its worker slot back instead of sitting on it. In the terminal, the sensor is tested alone for the thirty first. The marker is not there yet, so the task is marked up for reschedule: not failed, just not yet. Then the export finishes, here by hand, writing the empty marker into the night's folder. The sensor is tested again, finds it, and succeeds: Bronze may load. The side pane draws the loop: is it there; not yet, wait; there, go. The marker is the same idea as Course 5's sealed nights: a folder is complete only when it says so. Next, what happens when a task fails.

Some failures are a blip and some are a fact, and a nightly job must tell them apart. The output is mocked. The editor shows the D A G's defaults. Every task may be retried twice, a minute apart: enough for a busy service to recover, not enough to hide a real problem for long. A failure emails the team, and an S L A marks the night late if a task hasn't finished four hours after the schedule. In the terminal, the whole D A G is tested for the thirty first. The sensor passes. Bronze's first try fails: BigQuery answers five oh three, a temporary error. A minute later the second try succeeds, and the night carries on: G2, Silver, the guide, G3. Then gate three fails. G3's verdict for the night is false, the guide's gap from Course 8, and it is false on every try, so after three tries the task is failed, the team is emailed, and everything after it is marked upstream failed. Gold is not built on a night the gates rejected. The side pane lists each task's tries and state, and the difference: a blip is retried away, a fact stays failed. Next, fixing the night.

The night failed at gate three, and the fix belongs to whoever owns the data: the guide's vendor. The output is mocked. The vendor delivers the guide again, with the missing slot for SUN MOVIES two. It can't replace the first delivery: the raw zone keeps every object for its retention period, so the new file has a new name, r two. The editor shows the change that lets that work: the guide loader now takes the night's latest delivery, by name. In the terminal the new file lands. Then, rather than rerunning the whole night, only the guide's task is cleared, with everything downstream of it. The listing shows exactly what will run again: the guide, G3 and its check, Gold, the Spark batch, G4 and its check. The D A G is run again, those tasks succeed, and the run ends green. The audit table tells the whole story, because no verdict is ever overwritten: G2 passed, G3 failed twice and then passed with no minute uncovered, and G4, failed once in Course 10 by the planted bug, now passes. The side pane draws the night going red, the fix, and green. Next, running nights again on purpose.

Sometimes past nights must be run again: a bug fixed, a rule changed, a late delivery. That is a backfill, and it is only safe if running a night twice gives the same tables as running it once. The output is mocked. The editor shows Bronze's script as it now begins: delete the night, then insert it. Every layer does the same, keyed by the run's night: Bronze, the quarantine, Silver, Gold, and the Spark batch's partition overwrite. In the terminal, the D A G is backfilled for the thirty first, resetting the existing run. Thirteen tasks succeed. A query counts the night through every layer: four hundred and one thousand, nine hundred and fifty eight rows in Bronze, seven quarantined, four hundred thousand, nine hundred and forty nine in Silver, three hundred and seventy thousand and forty one minutes in Gold, and twelve exchanges. Then the backfill runs again, and every number is the same. Without the deletes, the second run would have doubled Bronze, and G4 would have caught it, but only after the damage. The side pane shows the pattern: delete the night, insert it again, and a rerun changes nothing. Next, where this D A G would run for real.

On a laptop, Airflow stops when the laptop does. In production it runs as Cloud Composer, Google's managed Airflow. The output is mocked, and nothing here was applied. The editor shows the Terraform module. Composer three's environment runs the same image version this course used locally, Airflow two point ten point five, with the Google provider pinned. It is the smallest size, and its workers act as s a airflow, the D A G's own service account made in Course 4. One grant comes first: Composer's service agent needs its own role on the project. In the terminal Terraform plans only this module: two resources to add, the grant and the environment. The plan stops there on purpose. A Composer environment bills for every hour it exists, whether or not a D A G is running, and this course runs one night. Applying it would be the same plan with apply, and the D A G folder would be copied into the environment's bucket. The side pane shows what Google would run: the scheduler, the workers, the web server and the database, patched and scaled, with the same D A G file. Next, a look back at the three ways the platform remembers its progress.

Every part of viewing pulse can stop halfway: a reader crashes, a job is drained, a night fails. Each lane remembers its progress differently, and each needs its own answer to the same question: after a restart, is anything lost, and is anything counted twice? This frame is a model, a summary of the last six courses, and each claim points at the section that showed it. Pub Sub remembers with the acknowledgement. A message stays until a reader acknowledges it, so a reader that dies is sent it again, and a restart can repeat messages; that is why every lane deduplicates by event I D. Dataflow remembers with the watermark and window state, kept by the service; a drain closes the open windows before stopping, and data later than the allowed lateness is dropped on purpose. The batch remembers with the partition. A night is a date, sealed by its success marker, and Airflow's run is that night; running it again replaces the night, never appends to it. Three mechanisms, one rule: a restart may repeat work, so the work must be safe to repeat. Next course, the last: protecting the data, watching it, and shipping changes safely.

The C R M holds every household's email and phone number. Analysts need households; almost nobody needs to contact them. The output is mocked. The editor shows column-level security in Terraform. A taxonomy, sun p i i, names what Sun treats as sensitive. A policy tag inside it, contact, means a way to reach a person. Only one group, p i i readers, is granted fine-grained read on that tag. Then Silver gains a households table, and its email and phone columns carry the tag. In the terminal, the table is filled with the night's five thousand households. A query for household, region and exchange works as always. The same query asking for email is refused, naming the tag and the column. Priya owns this project and is still refused: access to a tagged column is granted per tag, never inherited from a role on the table or the project. The side pane draws the chain: taxonomy, tag, column, reader. The table stays useful to everyone; the two columns that identify a person stay with the few who need them. Next, the same data as a file, outside BigQuery.

Policy tags protect a column in BigQuery. A C S V extract in a bucket has no columns to tag, and extracts get copied, attached and shared. Sensitive Data Protection finds what is personal in any text, and can rewrite it. The output is mocked. The editor shows a small script. It reads the night's households extract from the raw zone and sends it to the service as a table, asking for three kinds of information: email addresses, phone numbers and people's names, reported only when likely or surer. In the terminal the inspection finds them where they are: five thousand emails, five thousand phone numbers, and a person's name in both name columns. The second step de-identifies: every finding is replaced by the name of its kind. The first rows of the redacted file show it: names, email and phone become their labels, while household, postcode and region survive, so the file still serves analysis. The side pane follows a finding from inspection to the masked file. Next, the question every auditor asks first: where did this number come from?

When the derby's audience is questioned, someone has to show where it came from. Nobody kept that map by hand, and nobody needed to. The output is mocked. Dataplex records lineage automatically: every BigQuery job that writes a table leaves a link from the tables it read. The editor shows a script that walks those links backwards. For a table, it asks the lineage A P I for every link that ends there, prints each source, and walks on from it, until it reaches files. In the terminal, Gold's content table leads back to four sources: the households and titles read in place from the raw zone, the subscriber dimension, and Silver's viewing events. Silver leads to Bronze, Bronze to the external table, and that to the device platform's export in the raw bucket. The quarantine appears too, because Silver reads it to leave the bad rows out. The side pane draws the longest path, from the raw files to Gold, and lists the other sources. Next, a different kind of check, kept beside the table instead of inside the D A G.

The gates live inside the nightly D A G. Dataplex offers another place for rules: a data quality scan, kept and reported beside the table itself. The output is mocked. The editor shows a scan of Silver's viewing events for the night, in Terraform, with four rules: every event has an I D, no I D appears twice, the platform is one of Sun's four names, and seconds watched lie between zero and sixty. In the terminal the scan runs on demand, and its result comes back: four hundred thousand, nine hundred and forty nine rows, and every rule passed. The comment above the scan says why the gates did not move here. G2 checks titles against the catalogue, G3 checks the guide against the minutes, G4 checks Gold against Silver: each compares two tables, and a scan looks at one. The side pane sorts the rules by where they belong. A rule about one table's own shape fits a scan, visible to anyone browsing the catalog. A rule that compares tables stays a gate, where it can stop the night. Next, watching the platform as it runs.

Every BigQuery job writes an audit entry when it finishes: who ran it, what it was, and how many bytes it billed. Those entries pass through the log router into Cloud Logging, kept thirty days by default. The output is mocked. The editor shows a saved log query. It asks for finished BigQuery jobs whose labels name the viewing daily D A G, from the night's run. The labels came for free: Airflow's BigQuery operator tags every job with the D A G and task that started it. In the terminal, the query and a table format are read from files, and the night's six jobs come back in order, from Bronze to G4, each with the task that ran it and the bytes it billed. Bronze is the largest, reading the raw files in full; the gates bill BigQuery's ten megabyte minimum. Nothing here was built for monitoring: the platform already explained itself, and a query found it. The side pane draws the path from job, to router, to the query. Next, being told when something is wrong, instead of looking.

During a match, nobody is reading logs. If the live count goes wrong, someone must be told. The output is mocked. The editor shows one alert policy in Terraform. Its metric is the age of the oldest message on Dataflow's subscription that nobody has acknowledged yet. While the job keeps up, that age stays at seconds. If the job stops, or falls behind, it climbs. The condition opens an incident when the age is over three hundred seconds for two minutes, so a single slow moment doesn't wake anyone. The notification goes to the email channel made with the budget in Course 3, and the documentation field tells whoever reads it the first command to run. In the terminal, Terraform adds the policy, and the list of alert policies shows it enabled. The incident closes itself when the job catches up. The side pane draws the chain: the metric, the policy, the channel. It watches the one thing a viewer would notice: a live number that has stopped moving. Next, the same platform, twice.

Everything so far lived in one project, sun media dev. Production is a second project, built by the same code. The output is mocked, and nothing was applied to production. The editor shows all that production needs of its own: a variables file saying prod, and the region. Every module stays exactly as it is. In the terminal, the project variable points at sun media prod, and Terraform is initialised against that project's own state bucket, with reconfigure, so the two states can never mix. The plan for production lists every resource the courses built, to add, and nothing to change or destroy. That plan is the same code reviewed twice: once against dev, where it was applied and tested, and once against prod. Workspaces are not used, and the terminal shows it: separate state buckets in separate projects keep a mistaken command in one environment from touching the other. The side pane shows one root module, two projects, and the table of what differs: only the variables and the state. Next, making every change go through the same checks before anyone applies it.

A change to viewing pulse should never reach a project because someone remembered to check it. Cloud Build runs the checks on every push. The output is mocked. The editor shows the build file. It runs as s a c i c d, the service account made for this in Course 4, in four steps: Terraform's format check, a validation of the configuration, a lint of every S Q L file in the warehouse, and finally a plan against dev, written into the build's log. There is no apply step, on purpose. C I proposes; a person reads the plan and applies it. In the terminal, the build is submitted by hand to show it end to end: the source is uploaded, the four steps run, the plan reports no changes, and the build succeeds in a little over two minutes. In production, a trigger connected to the GitHub repository starts the same build on every push to main. The side pane follows a push from GitHub, through the build, to a plan waiting for review. Next, the end of the film, and what could be built on top of all this.

Twelve courses ago, Sun had a derby and two questions. On the left is what answers them now. The live lane: every box's events through Pub Sub into a Dataflow job, counting households minute by minute while the match plays. The nightly lane: the night's files landed, sealed and kept, judged by gates, cleaned into Silver and summarised into Gold. Around both, Airflow runs the night, policy tags and de-identification protect the households, lineage and alerts explain and watch it, and every change goes through a reviewed plan. This frame is a model of what comes next, and nothing on the right was built. No machine learning appears in this film. With clean, trusted data, three things become possible. Predicting which households might leave, from their package history and viewing. Recommending what to watch next, from Silver's viewing. And personalising the screen while the match is on, fed by the live lane. Each would sit on top of what was built here, in BigQuery or Vertex AI, and each would only be as good as the data underneath. The derby peaked at two thousand one hundred and forty households at eighteen forty one, and one London exchange explained the complaints.
